title: Inference stack tipping points and sales hooks
content:
Purpose:
This is a practical notes-and-hooks brief for SEs and growth reps when evaluating customers considering self-hosted inference stacks (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM families) vs Redwood hosted/dedicated/private. Focus: concrete tipping points, reproducible questions to surface, and ready-to-use talking points that map directly to operator pain and procurement signals.

Audience:
- Sales Engineers, Growth AEs, Solutions Engineers, GTM PMs.

TL;DR (elevator):
Most customers choose to build when they believe they can materially reduce per-token cost and control latency at scale. They underestimate the ongoing ops burden (patching, kernel tuning, model rollouts, KV cache correctness, autoscaling policies) and the fragility of homemade fallbacks. Bring up these tipping points early: predictable SLOs, end-to-end observability, easy model swaps, and economic break-even windows (6–18 months) — those are our hooks.

Key differentiation framing (concise):
- Cost: Self-hosted wins on sticker GPU-only token cost at very high steady throughput (>10M tokens/day sustained) and full M40/T4-style utilization. Redwood wins on end-to-end unit economics once you include maintenance, downtime, underutilization, and staff costs.
- Latency & Throughput: vLLM/TGI can beat naive hosted endpoints for single-model, single-tenant bursts; Redwood beats them for multi-model, multi-tenant workloads via smart routing, batching, and KV caching.
- Risk & Reliability: Homegrown stacks have brittle fallback logic during OOMs, software regressions, and kernel incompatibilities. Redwood provides canary rollouts, automatic routing to compatible variants, and SLA-backed fallbacks.
- Time-to-value: Expect 2–6 months to validate an MVP self-hosted stack (with mature infra team); Redwood hosted API produces results in hours.

Practical tipping points / diagnostic questions to ask customers:
(Use these to map to a buy decision or create urgency)
1) "What's your current or expected 95th-percentile per-request latency SLA?" — If they require <50ms L95 across global regions, ask about multi-region orchestration.
2) "What steady-state token throughput do you expect (tokens/day)?" — If <1M tokens/day, managed is almost always cheaper when you factor staff.
3) "How many distinct model variants and prompt templates will you serve?" — >5 variants => heavy consistency and rollout burdens for self-hosted.
4) "Do you have staff time dedicated to GPU kernel debugging, quantization regressions, and nightly model health runs?" — If no, the ops cost is material.
5) "What is your tolerance for 1–3 hour incidents during model upgrades or OOM storms?" — Many infra teams underweight this impact.
6) "Are you subject to compliance constraints that require air-gapped or customer-managed keys?" — If yes, private deployment path is viable; highlight Redwood Private.

Operator pain-map (notes to bring into demo/SE call):
- Patching and kernel drift: new CUDA/cuDNN updates break float->quantized kernels unpredictably.
- Unbounded tail latencies: extreme variance during cache misses and cold KV lookups.
- Silent quality regressions after quantization or pruning; no easy A/B test harness.
- Autoscaler thrash: naive queueing leads to oscillations and cost spikes.
- Cross-team friction: data science wants new weights, infra resists cluster config changes.

Quantitative example (simple TCO thought experiment to use on call):
Assumptions: 2M tokens/day steady, peak 5M/day, 2 models, 1 SRE (0.2 FTE), 1 ML engineer (0.25 FTE) for ops.
- Raw on-prem GPU cost (amortized + depreciation): $1.2M/year => $100k/month for a modest cluster that can hold peaks.
- Staff cost loaded: 0.45 FTE ~ $80k/year (loaded) => ~$6.6k/month.
- Opportunity / downtime risk, upgrades, and inefficiencies estimate: +20% overhead on top of raw cost.
Result: fully-burdened cost often converges to parity with Redwood hosted once you include staff and risk windows within 9–14 months. Use this as a heuristic: customers who expect to exceed 12–18 months of heavy steady throughput OR require strict isolation are better candidates for self-hosted.

Specific technical comparisons (phrases SEs can use):
- vLLM/TGI: Excellent for building a focused, single-model stack quickly. Be explicit about KV eviction semantics, memory compaction strategies, and their maintenance needs.
- TensorRT-LLM: Great latency profile with INT8 quantization but heavy engineering effort to get stable quantized accuracy on custom models; expect a model-retracing cycle for each major update.
- Hybrid approach customers try: vLLM for dev/prod parity + TensorRT for a narrow, latency-critical path. Call this the ‘two-tier’ trap — it doubles rollout complexity and hidden ops.

Sales hooks mapped to customer signals:
- If customer complains about "surprising token bills": lead with caching and prefix reuse capabilities, cost attribution at the token level, and Redwood Optimize recommendations.
- If customer has minimal infra staff: lead with "time to production" and the managed SLA.
- If customer is security/constrained: highlight Redwood Private, KMS integrations, and audited rollouts.
- If customer is switching from a naive self-hosted PoC: emphasize observability gaps (per-route latency breakdown, token-level chargeback) and the rollback/canary tooling.

Objections & suggested rebuttals (copy-paste friendly):
1) "We can run it cheaper ourselves."
   - Response: "Totally reasonable if you have steady, very high throughput and low churn in model versions. Two things to watch: the ops headcount and the risk of a 1–2 day outage during kernel/driver upgrades. We can build a 9–12 month cost model together that includes staff and incident risk — typically that’s the clarifying moment."
2) "We need full control over model weights and inference path."
   - Response: "We support Private deployments and bring the same dev experience + observability. Many customers start with Private to meet control needs and later migrate to Reserved/Dedicated as confidence grows."
3) "Quantized accuracy will suffer if we don't manage everything ourselves."
   - Response: "Redwood Optimize provides quantization profiles tied to your evals and A/B rollback safety nets — we automate the tuning loops most teams invest months in."

SE playbook checklist (call/POC-friendly):
- Pre-call: ask for expected tokens/day, model count, SLAs, and current infra org chart.
- On call: surface at least 3 operational risks we can solve (observability, autoscale, rollouts).
- Demo: show per-route token breakdown, a canary rollback, and Optimize suggestions for quantization/batching.
- POC scope: target a single critical path (e.g., chat front-end) and measure latency, cost, and error rate for 2 weeks.

Email template (intro to technical buyer):
Subject: Quick check — inference SLOs and ops pain
Hi <Name>,
Following up from our conversation: two quick questions that will help scope a short POC and economic model: 1) what steady and peak tokens/day do you expect? 2) who owns day-to-day infra and how many FTEs? If you prefer, we can run a quick model with your numbers and show the 9–12 month break-even.
Thanks,
Asha (Redwood SE)

Playbook for pricing conversations (practical knobs):
- If customer needs predictable throughput: offer Dedicated with a 6–12 month commit and show guaranteed latency profiles.
- If the customer wants to “test the water”: propose a short Reserved trial for critical routes + pay-as-you-go for the rest.
- For regulated customers: lead with Private + managed console + optional SRE services for the initial 90-day onboarding.

Uncommon signals that usually indicate imminent build:
- They already have GPU headcount earmarked on Q4 hiring plan (~2+ engineers).
- Legal has greenlit air-gapped deployments and they have finished a rack-level procurement checklist.
- They have a latency SLA tied to revenue (e.g., customer-facing chat where >200ms L95 reduces conversions).

Next steps for GTM team:
- Create an internal one-pager TCO template that SEs can fill during discovery (inputs: tokens/day, models, peak ratio, FTEs, desired SLA).
- Build a demo script that reproduces a common self-hosted failure (OOM + miss-route) and show Redwood’s automatic fallback in the Console.
- Run a win/loss audit for the last 12 months to extract real break-even points and update this doc.

Notes / scratch area (things to iterate on):
- Add model-specific numbers (Llama2-family vs Mistral vs Llama3) around memory footprint after quantization.
- Put an example of a two-week POC metrics dashboard we can drop into customer decks.

End of brief.
